title: Determinants II: Row Reduction & Properties
description: Evaluate determinants by row reduction, then apply the key properties (transpose, row operations, scaling, products, invertibility) to predict a determinant without recomputing it (Anton §2.2–2.3).

questions.prompt: Evaluate by row reduction (cofactor expansion gives the same answer): $\det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$
questions.explanation: Row-reduce to triangular form and multiply the diagonal (tracking any swaps/scalings), or expand by cofactors along any row/column — either way, $\det = 15$.

questions.prompt: Evaluate by row reduction (cofactor expansion gives the same answer): $\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
questions.explanation: Row-reduce to triangular form and multiply the diagonal (tracking any swaps/scalings), or expand by cofactors along any row/column — either way, $\det = -6$.

questions.explanation: Row-reduce to triangular form and multiply the diagonal (tracking any swaps/scalings), or expand by cofactors along any row/column — either way, $\det = 18$.

questions.explanation: Row-reduce to triangular form and multiply the diagonal (tracking any swaps/scalings), or expand by cofactors along any row/column — either way, $\det = 15$.

questions.prompt: You swap two rows of a matrix. What happens to the determinant?
explanations: A row swap is exactly the operation that flips the sign — the determinant does change.
Swapping rows doesn't scale the determinant, it flips its sign.
Swapping rows never forces the determinant to 0 unless it already was.

questions.prompt: You perform the row replacement $R_2 \to R_2 + 5R_1$ on a matrix. What happens to the determinant?
explanations: Row replacement (adding a multiple of one row to another) is the one operation that leaves the determinant completely unchanged.
Sign flips come from swapping rows, not from a row replacement.
Row replacement doesn't scale the determinant at all.

questions.prompt: You scale row 2 of a matrix by $-3$. If the original determinant was 8, what is the new determinant?
explanations: Scaling a row does change the determinant — it's not left alone.
The sign of the scale factor carries through: scaling by $-3$ multiplies the determinant by $-3$, not $3$.
The full factor of $-3$ applies, not just a sign flip.

questions.prompt: True or False: $\det(A^T) = \det(A)$ for any square matrix $A$.
explanations: Transposing swaps rows and columns, but every determinant property that holds for rows also holds for columns — the determinant is unchanged.

questions.prompt: A $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ has $\det(A) = 4$. What is $\det(2A)$?
explanations: Doubling every entry scales all 3 rows, not just one — so the factor is $2^3$, not $2$.
Close, but the exponent should match the size of the matrix: $2^3$, not $2^2$.
$\det(2A) \ne \det(A)$ — scaling the whole matrix does change the determinant.

questions.prompt: $\det(A) = 5$ and $\det(B) = -3$ for two $n\times n$ matrices. What is $\det(AB)$?
explanations: Determinants multiply here, they don't add.
Watch the sign — $5 \times (-3) = -15$, not $15$.
Determinants multiply under matrix multiplication, they don't subtract.

questions.prompt: True or False: if $\det(A) \ne 0$, then $A$ is invertible.
explanations: A nonzero determinant is exactly the invertibility test — row reduction always reaches a full set of nonzero pivots in this case.

questions.prompt: $\det(A) = 0$ for a square matrix $A$. What can you conclude?
choices: A must be the zero matrix
explanations: It's the opposite — a zero determinant rules out invertibility.
Plenty of nonzero matrices have determinant 0 — having a repeated or dependent row is enough.
The invertibility property gives a definite answer here: not invertible.

questions.prompt: $\det(A) = 6$ for an invertible matrix $A$. What is $\det(A^{-1})$?
explanations: That's $\det(A)$ itself, not $\det(A^{-1})$.
There's no sign flip involved here.
$A^{-1}$ exists and is itself invertible, so its determinant can't be 0.

questions.prompt: A matrix has two identical rows. What must its determinant be?
explanations: Two identical rows force a very specific value, not this one.
This one is fully determined by the fact that two rows match — no other entries matter.
It's perfectly computable — and it's always the same value.

questions.prompt: True or False: for square matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same size, $\det(AB) = \det(BA)$, even though $AB \ne BA$ in general.
explanations: $\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B) = \det(B)\det(A) = \det(BA)$ — ordinary number multiplication commutes even when matrix multiplication doesn't.

questions.prompt: You take the transpose of a matrix, then take the transpose again: $(A^T)^T$. What is $\det\big((A^T)^T\big)$ compared to $\det(A)$?
explanations: Transposing never flips a determinant's sign on its own.
Transposing doesn't square anything.
$(A^T)^T = A$ exactly, so this is fully determined.
